source.title: Dynamics of Transient Structure in In-Context Linear Regression Transformers
source.authors: Liam Carroll; Jesse Hoogland; Matthew Farrugia-Roberts; Daniel Murfet

record.file_problem: The full paper is present, including appendices. Some figure content is flattened or not numerically legible in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses grokking, but its experiments concern the reverse transition—transient generalization followed by specialization—in in-context linear regression. It does not test any listed version of the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper cites grokking and reports its own transient-ridge results. Those results concern a different task and transition direction, so they do not test the listed versions. Rows below record related findings, not evidence for or against those versions.
record.test_reason: The study's experiments concern transient ridge in in-context linear regression: a generalizing solution that later gives way to memorization (the reverse of grokking). It cites grokking (Power et al., Nanda et al.) only as a contrasting example. It runs no algorithmic grokking experiments and measures no delayed generalization after training saturation. It does not vary weight decay (set to 0) or init scale, and does not compare algorithms across seeds for a grokking task. Its results do not bear on V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that intermediate-diversity transformers transiently approximate ridge before specializing to dMMSE. Joint trajectory PCA reveals generalization versus memorization as a principal axis of development. An evolving loss/LLC tradeoff, akin to Bayesian internal model selection, is consistent with this. Why transience stops above the task-diversity threshold is left open. They also note that their tradeoff does not account for complexity-decreasing transitions such as grokking.
record.recipe_differences: Uses synthetic in-context linear regression tasks with varying task diversity, mean-squared-error training, and OOD loss, trajectory PCA, and LLC analyses. It does not reproduce modular-arithmetic grokking or measure training accuracy and test accuracy as in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Task diversity changes the trajectory and whether transient ridge appears; architecture size slightly changes the task-diversity threshold. Trajectory PCA also differs with checkpoint sampling strategy.

fits_no_version.finding: At intermediate task diversity (M=16–128), OOD loss first falls toward ridge, then rises to dMMSE. This is a transient generalizing solution replaced by memorization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transformers trained for in-context linear regression at intermediate task diversity transiently generalize (ridge) before specializing to the training tasks (dMMSE).

fits_no_version.finding: LLC estimates of fully trained low-M models rise with M and cross the ridge LLC near the onset of transience. Some intermediate-M models show LLC spikes near the minimum OOD loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An evolving loss/complexity (LLC) tradeoff is consistent with transient generalization-to-memorization transitions.

fits_no_version.finding: The step of minimum OOD loss tends to increase with task diversity within the transient range.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The timing of transient ridge shifts later as task diversity grows.

record.problems: The main OOD evaluation uses a fixed dataset of 512 samples. Loss and trajectory curves are lightly smoothed. The study reports no uncertainty intervals for the results summarized here. The M = 182 and M = 256 runs were still decreasing slowly at the end of training; some LLC chains/checkpoints are described as underconverged. The paper notes that the causal explanation remains uncertain.
record.rows_left_out: The paper gives individual tcritM values in Appendix B.2 and additional architecture-specific curves in Appendix I; these were not separately rowed because they are measurements of transient ridge, not of any listed claim version. Figure-only numerical curve values were not transcribed.

untested.parts: All of V1: no algorithmic datasets, no train/test accuracy gap, no dependence of the delay on training-set size.
All of V2: no circuit analysis or progress measures for a grokking transition.
All of V3: no manipulation of initialization scale or weight norm, and no delayed generalization on non-algorithmic data.
All of V4: no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
All of V5: weight decay is 0, and there is no critical dataset size or ungrokking test. The LLC complexity account concerns the reverse transition.
All of V6: a single seed, and no comparison of algorithms across runs.
All of V7: no optimizer or numerical-precision controls.

record.verdict_notes: The paper explicitly calls grokking the reverse phenomenon. It notes its loss/complexity tradeoff does not account for transitions that decrease complexity, as grokking does. Training uses Adam with no weight decay. No verdicts are given, because no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test delayed generalization after training accuracy saturates on small algorithmic datasets, or how that delay depends on training-set size.
It does not study gradual formation of a grokking generalizing circuit, removal of memorizing components, or progress measures anticipating a grokking jump.
It does not test grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic data or manipulate initialization scale or weight norm to switch such delays.
It does not study realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning.
It studies a loss/complexity account of transient ridge, but does not test whether low norm favors a more efficient grokking circuit, or the claimed critical dataset size and ungrokking behavior.
It does not identify or compare algorithms learned across runs of the same task.
It does not test whether grokking is an optimizer or numerical artifact.
